note:
Title of the book. See Introduction: Title and Author; Date and Occasion.

**oracle ... vision.** “Oracle” focuses more on the contents of a weighty prophecy of judgment (Hab. 1:1 note), whereas “vision” relates to the process by which God communicates to the prophet’s inner perception.

**Nineveh.** In Nahum’s day, it is the capital city of the Assyrian Empire and situated on the east bank of the river Tigris at its confluence with the river Khosr. Repeatedly, it is described as “a great city” in Jon. 1:2; 3:2–4; 4:11. Here, Nineveh stands for Assyria as a whole and conveys the idea of evil forces arrayed against the people of God.

The introductory hymn (vv. 2–8), which in the Hebrew forms an incomplete acrostic poem, movingly describes the Lord as the Judge of all, with power to accomplish His will.

**1:2, 3** The Lord’s character forms the key to what follows. The repetition of “the LORD” emphasizes that it is the God of the covenant who is described.

**1:2 jealous.** This attribute refers to God’s passionate reaction against any infringement on His holiness or any attempt to share His glory. His jealousy demands undivided loyalty and reveals itself as wrath against rejection of Him or His lordship.

**avenging ... avenging ... takes vengeance.** True to His nature, the universal Judge leaves no sin unpunished and metes out the just deserts of the wicked (Deut. 32:35). The threefold repetition of the Hebrew word for “avenge” strongly emphasizes an inescapable and appropriate retribution.

**adversaries ... enemies.** Those who oppose God’s sovereign reign over the whole earth.

**1:3 slow to anger.** A well-known confession of God’s patience with sinners (Ex. 34:6; Jon. 4:2).

**great in power ... by no means clear.** God’s patience never implies that He is weak or that He condones evil (Gen. 18:25; Ex. 34:7).

The prophet offers a poetic portrayal of the power of the Lord as manifested in His control of nature on occasions of intervention in behalf of His people (Ex. 14:21, 22; Ps. 18:7–15; Matt. 8:26). The godly Israelite recognizes the Lord’s work in nature. But nature is not confused with God or worshiped as God; it is the theater of His revelation.

These words vividly portray the power of God in subjecting the forces of nature, as at the crossing of the Red Sea (Ex. 14).

**sea ... rivers.** Used here as poetic parallels (Is. 50:2; Ps. 74:12–15). The fertile pastures of Bashan to the northeast of Judah, the vineyards of Carmel to the northwest, and the forests of Lebanon to the north all wither when the hot desert wind, sent by the Lord, blows over them (Is. 33:9).

The displeasure of the approaching Lord fills the earth and its creatures with terror. All creation seems threatened when even the seemingly permanent things (“the mountains ... the earth”) tremble and disappear.
The rhetorical questions emphasize the irresistibility of God’s anger. Divine wrath is compared to fire (Deut. 4:24; Ps. 11:6; Heb. 12:29).

Whereas the subject matter of vv. 4**–**6 concerned nature, the focus now returns to God and His enemies (vv. 2, 3).

**1:7 good.** The term denotes the Lord’s benevolence as the source of all true human well-being and prosperity, and is particularly a confession of His abundant covenant blessings and kindness (Ps. 73:1). The Lord’s people experience His awesome power as holy love. When help is needed He is an impregnable fortress (Ps. 46).

Striking images of severe, all-encompassing judgment. The metaphor of a flood is used in Is. 8:6 of an invading army, but here it might literally anticipate what actually contributes to Nineveh’s collapse (2:6).

**of the adversaries.** A wordplay, since this may also be heard as “of her place,” most probably hinting at Nineveh—brought out more fully below.

The downfall of the wicked, represented by Nineveh, will culminate in the comfort of God’s people, Judah.

**1:9 plot.** All Assyrian strategies will be futile. Their struggle and their plans are against the Lord, who has decided on their destruction and will bring it about once and for all (Ps. 2).

Perhaps a reference to Ashurbanipal (see Introduction: Date and Occasion), or, more probably, to Sennacherib, the most powerful Assyrian aggressor against Judah (2 Kin. 18:13–18). “From you” is a feminine form referring to the city of Nineveh.

**worthless.** The Hb. word suggests something demonic.

A comforting divine message assures God’s people that the downfall of Assyria implies the end of their humiliation.

**1:12 Thus says the LORD** . A well-known prophetic-messenger formula. “They” refers to the Assyrians, and “you” to Judah.

verse_quote: break his yoke ... burst your bonds.
note: Vivid poetic images of emancipation (Jer. 2:20; Ps. 2:3). God will break the power of the Assyrian oppressor.

The word emphasizes authority and certainty. “You” possibly refers to the Assyrian emperor, whose fate reflects that of the nation as a whole.

**your name.** The elimination of one’s name from memory reflects common Near Eastern curse formulas. Complete loss of power and prestige awaits the Assyrians.

**house of your gods.** The temple and other objects of Assyria’s trust and pride will also be destroyed.

**grave.** The term denotes the final undoing of Nineveh, its king, and its people in 612 B.C.

This section is written in the prophetic present tense. Events still future are pictured as if already present, and events even more distantly future are portrayed as occurring at the same time with those happening much earlier. This vivid prophecy of judgment is a poetic “vision” (1:1; cf. Num. 12:6–8), and is not a precise and detailed historical account of events that later take place in 612 B.C.

**1:15–2:2** See Is. 52:7. The approach of a herald of “good news,” whose feet tread “the mountains” of Judah, will initiate a new period of grateful service to the Lord. The good news is summarized in the meaningful word “peace” (Hb. _shalom_), signifying not only the end of hostilities but also the return to normal, abundant living conditions and general well-being. This passage, together with Is. 53:1, is picked up by the apostle Paul in Rom. 10:15, 16.

**Keep ... vows.** Periods of national crisis or foreign oppression often make celebration of the important temple feasts difficult, if not impossible, during the old covenant era. The “vows” made in the previous period of distress should now be fulfilled (Ps. 116:14, 17–19).

In sharp contrast to the call for Judah to celebrate, Nahum resumes his address to Nineveh with the ironic exhortation that it should prepare for an attack.

**has come.** Nahum speaks as one whose “vision” (v. 1) permits him to be an eyewitness of the attack on Nineveh.

**scatterer.** The Assyrians, who have destroyed many nations, including Israel, by scattering them over the face of the earth, will experience a similar fate. In August 612 B.C., the combined forces of the Medes and Babylonians destroyed Nineveh, and shortly afterward the Assyrian Empire collapsed.

God will restore the oppressed people to the happiness implied by the name “Israel.” Jacob received this new name as a sign of his spiritual maturity and his willing acceptance of the destiny God intended for him from the beginning (Gen. 32:27, 28).

Probably a reference to the Lord’s army (v. 2). The warriors and chariots of the attackers will fulfill His purposes. The armies of Assyria herself earlier were God’s instruments to accomplish His purposes of judgment (Is. 10:5–7).

**red ... scarlet.** These terms emphasize the awe-inspiring appearance of the approaching army, whether the color refers to their actual robes or to the bloodstains on them. Red colors were favored by the Babylonian army (Ezek. 23:14).

**spears are brandished.** The Hebrew is difficult but conveys the general impression of ready eagerness for war.

Nineveh is a beehive of frantic soldiers.

**streets.** Possibly open fields or plains outside the city; if so, the verse speaks of the approaching army and its chariots of war.

This may refer to the Assyrian king and his nobles, especially the military commanders. Alternatively, this verse may describe the attackers and their frenzied siege of Nineveh. The Hb. word here rendered “siege tower” usually refers to a movable structure shielding the besiegers of a city, technically known as a “mantelet” (text note).

The city of Nineveh was on the bank of the Tigris River, and a smaller river flowed through the city. Conflicting ancient accounts ascribe the fall of Nineveh to flooding when the enemy redirected the dams and sluices of the water system. The description in Nahum is manifestly poetic, however. The term “gates” could simply refer to the five gates opening (cf. 3:13) in the direction of the Tigris River with its tributaries and canals.

**palace.** The seat of political and military organization.

Nineveh is personified as a woman, a queen, going into exile. Her “slave girls,” the inhabitants of the city, mourn the fate of their mistress. Alternatively, “she” might refer to the goddess Ishtar, whose image is taken as plunder while the girls who served in her temple bewail their loss.
This striking image is often taken to portray Nineveh’s full population and prosperity. Now it is drained away.

verse_quote: Plunder the silver, plunder the gold!
note: The Assyrian royal annals make numerous references to plunder being taken from conquered cities.
The merciless devastation creates terror and paralysis among the once-mighty Ninevites.

This closing section is a taunt song in which the striking image of a pride of lions that meets with destruction is employed to describe the imminent reversal of Nineveh’s fortunes. God is the author of Nineveh’s humiliation and disappearance.

**2:11 Where.** This rhetorical question emphasizes how the famous city will be reduced to oblivion.

**the lions’** **den.** An apt image for Nineveh as the home of the aggressive and ruthless Assyrians, particularly since extant Assyrian texts often pre­sent the king as a lion.

The real secret of Nineveh’s full and final downfall is revealed. Confrontation with Israel’s almighty covenant God is fatal to the Assyrian Empire.

**I am against you.** The opposite of the good tidings of salvation, “I will be with you” (Ex. 3:12; Josh. 1:5; Is. 43:2, 5).

**messengers.** The voices of the Assyrian envoys dictating terms and exacting tribute will be permanently silenced from the face of the earth.

The expression of woe that opens this chapter controls its mood until the last verse. The various parts all contribute to its literary unity, and together they emphasize the irreversible doom of Nineveh. The prophet no longer focuses on Israel and Judah alone, but places the fate of Nineveh in a universal perspective.

**3:1–7** These vivid scenes of violence, death, and destruction confirm the city’s expected doom. The charges against Nineveh (vv. 1–4) and her penalties (vv. 5–7) are set forth in stark detail.

**3:1 bloody city.** The phrase emphasizes the merciless cruelty openly boasted by the Assyrians in their official records.

**lies.** Deceitful diplomacy characterizes their international dealings (Is. 36:16, 17).

**plunder.** See 2:12, 13. Friendly negotiations serve as a cover for rapacious behavior. In their insatiable lust for more they have moved constantly from one victim to another.

These poetic verses provide one of the most vivid portrayals of a battle scene in the OT. The staccato beat, economy of words, and gruesome detail all contribute to the image of action that reduces whole populations to “heaps of corpses” (v. 3). Views differ as to whether this describes how Assyria conquered other nations, or, more probably, how enemy forces will assault Nineveh with a savagery that matches her own previous conduct., 3

With a change of imagery, Nineveh is likened to a beautiful and seductive “prostitute” for whose favor “nations” and “peoples” are sacrificed. Service of the gods, warfare, and commerce are closely intertwined. Seduction by Nineveh’s power and pomp implies apostasy from true religion and subjection to her “charms,” a term probably indicating the totality of pagan religion (Is. 47:12, 13).

Retribution by the universal Judge is inevitable. See 2:13.

**lift up your skirts.** The public humiliation by which harlots are punished in this era (Jer. 13:22; Hos. 2:3).
The image of the harlot is continued. She will be made an object of scorn and an example to deter others from doing the same.

The sight is so terrible that people will retreat from it in horror. So dreadful and truly deserved will be the disaster that no one will be found to mourn or comfort the nation in its downfall.

**who will grieve for her.** The rhetorical question expects the answer “no one” and emphasizes that even those who have reluctantly supported Nineveh will have no regrets at her downfall.

The fall of Thebes was a well-known event that marked the peak of Assyrian expansion. If such a city could be overwhelmed, it is presumptuous for Nineveh to assume that she is invincible.

**3:8 Thebes.** The Greek name for No-amon, the city of the Egyptian god Amon. This ancient and magnificent metropolis of Upper Egypt fell to the Assyrians in 663 B.C. Located on the Nile some four hundred miles (645 km) up the Nile valley from Memphis, it may have had moats and canals as defenses. There is probably a figurative element in Nahum’s emphasis on the sea. In Scripture, a river or sea is often an emblem for strength that only God can overcome (Ex. 15; Ps. 114:3–5; Is. 23:3, 4; Matt. 8:27). Alternatively, “sea” may be a Hebrew usage for any extensive body of inland water, such as the Nile, which was near Thebes (Is. 19:5).

The region to the south of Egypt.

**Egypt.** The land to the north of Thebes. Though its extensive resources had been available to defend Thebes, they were insufficient to avert disaster.

**Put.** Traditionally identified with Libya to the west, though others suggest an African location in the region of modern-day Somalia.

verse_quote: her infants were dashed in pieces.
note: Such brutal practices were carried out to deter future uprisings among subjugated peoples (cf. 2 Kin. 8:12; Ps. 137:9; Is. 13:16; Hos. 10:14).

Apparently a figurative reference to the cup of the Lord’s anger, from which all who defy Him are forced to drink (Is. 51:17–23; Lam. 4:21). Nineveh in her distress tries to hide and find refuge, but only the Lord provides refuge in times of trouble (1:7). Compared to Him, even the most powerful are weak and vulnerable (vv. 12–17).

**you will go into hiding.** This could also be translated “you will be concealed.” After its destruction in 612 B.C., the site of Nineveh remained abandoned until archaeological excavations commenced in the mid-nineteenth century A.D.
This telling image emphasizes that the normally impregnable fortresses are now not only desirable but also easy to take.
In the face of the approaching army, all the Assyrian troops are like women (i.e., not trained for warfare). All barriers to slow the enemy’s advance, such as gates and bars, have been removed.
Frantic efforts need to be made to “strengthen ... forts” and to prepare for a lengthy period of siege. The imperatives are ironic; vv. 14–17 reflect the mood of a derisive taunt song.
Even the most strenuous efforts to avoid invasion are useless. The city and its people succumb to fire and sword.

Assyria’s international trade and commerce bring people and wealth to Nineveh during the biblical era. Under pressure from outside, the self-interest of these traders has become clear. Having gathered like locusts, they seize what they can and disappear.

See text note. These two terms are rare in Hebrew and may be Assyrian loanwords. They probably represent important officials in the government of the vast empire. When things become dangerous they run away. Riches, power, and organization fail miserably as the nation collapses.

**sun rises.** The appearance of the Lord’s judgment will scatter His enemies as dramatically as the heat of day rouses and disperses sleeping locusts (cf. Ps. 84:11; Mal. 4:1–3).

The finality of divine judgment on the cruel oppressor will lead to universal rejoicing. These verses are reminiscent of funeral dirges and taunt songs of the period.

**3:18 shepherds.** A well-known metaphor for leaders indicates the subordinate rulers of the Assyrian king.

**asleep ... slumber.** Striking euphemisms for death.

**Your people ... gather them.** The pastoral image is extended to the people (or perhaps the army) as a flock of sheep. In the absence of shepherds, the people are scattered (cf. 1 Kin. 22:17).

**3:19** The “news” of Nineveh’s incurable “wound” and fatal “hurt” is received with general applause. The God of Israel, to whom alone vengeance belongs (Deut. 32:35; Rom. 12:19), finally puts an end to the continual wickedness that has caused such injustice and suffering. The vision of Nahum had its initial fulfillment in 612 B.C. but still awaits its final realization at the second coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
